questions.solution: Correct Option B: Horse ATG, rabbit ATG, Alemtuzumab The recommended first-line therapy for idiopathic aplastic anemia in patients who are not candidates for transplant is a combination of immunosuppressive agents. The most commonly used combination is horse anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) along with cyclosporine. Alemtuzumab, a monoclonal antibody, may also be used as an alternative to ATG. The sequence of therapy with horse ATG followed by rabbit ATG and then Alemtuzumab is based on the evidence that horse ATG has been shown to be more effective than rabbit ATG as an initial treatment for aplastic anemia. However, some patients may not respond adequately to horse ATG, and in such cases, an attempt with rabbit ATG can be made. BMP: Normal
Random Blood Glucose: 90 mg/dL
LFTS: Normal.
Iron studies: ferritin 975 ng/mL, serum iron 234 ug/dL, iron-binding capacity 265 ug/dL, and transferrin saturation 60%.
HFE genotyping revealed a homozygous C282Y genotype.

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Weekly phlebotomy: Hereditary hemochromatosis is a genetic disorder characterized by systemic iron overload. The major HFE mutation is C282Y, and approximately 15% of individuals of northern European origin are heterozygotes and 0.5% are homozygotes. C282Y heterozygotes do not develop disease. Approximately two-thirds of homozygotes for C282Y develop iron overload with elevated ferritin and markedly high transferrin saturation. Other HFE mutations are H63D and S65C. Compound heterozygotes (C282Y/H63D) may also develop hemochromatosis, but far less likely. The effect of S65C mutation is very minimal. HFE hemochromatosis is generally diagnosed in the fifth or sixth decade of life (in women after menopause). Clinical symptoms include fatigue, loss of libido, abdominal pain, and arthralgia. Cirrhosis of the liver, cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and endocrine dysfunction are frequent due to organ damage from iron accumulation. The fully penetrant form of the disease (bronze diabetes) is rarely seen. Treatment of HFE hemochromatosis in C282Y homozygotes is weekly phlebotomy to remove accumulated iron. Removal of 500 ml of blood removes approximately 200 mg of iron. Phlebotomy is recommended in individuals with iron overload even in the absence of end-organ damage. The goal is to reduce the ferritin to <100 ng/mL. Incorrect Options: Option A – Observation: Observation can be considered in C282Y homozygotes if the serum ferritin is normal or moderately elevated. In patients with markedly elevated ferritin, observation is not appropriate even in the absence of end-organ damage. Option B - Hepatic MRI to determine the liver iron content : Liver biopsy is not required in hereditary hemochromatosis when the diagnosis is established with genetic testing. Liver MRI is useful to estimate liver iron content (LIC) in patients with acquired hemochromatosis and is not necessary in HFE 282Y homozygotes with elevated ferritin. Option C - Oral deferasirox: Iron chelation is indicated in acquired forms of hemochromatosis due to multiple blood transfusions or ineffective hematopoiesis. Iron chelation is not required in HFE hemochromatosis because of the ease and efficacy of phlebotomy. However, iron chelation could be considered in patients who do not tolerate phlebotomy or in conjunction with phlebotomy in patients with massive iron overload and organ damage where rapid removal of iron may be needed. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D – All of the above: Poor oral iron absorption, non-compliance (most commonly due to gastrointestinal toxicity), and an additional, occult source of bleeding could all be responsible for her continued anaemia. After stabilization or treatment of active bleeding, oral iron supplementation is generally the initial means to replete iron stores in a hemodynamically stable patient with iron deficiency anaemia. Compared to infusion of iron, oral supplementation is generally less expensive and more readily available. Dosing is generally a total of 100 to 200 mg a day divided into 2 or 3 administrations. However, not all patients will respond appropriately and there is increasing data to support every other day supplementation of oral iron. A small (n=40) prospective study of oral iron supplementation on consecutive days versus alternate days demonstrated significantly higher cumulative fractional and cumulative total iron absorptions in the alternate days arm. Furthermore, they found no difference in once-daily dosing versus BID dosing. Please note that this was a small study and the optimal regimen for oral iron supplementation to treat anemia remains an area of investigation. Gastrointestinal (GI) toxicity occurs in ~70% of patients supplemented with oral iron. Symptoms can include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, epigastric discomfort, constipation, and dysgeusia. Such symptoms can contribute to patient non-compliance. Additionally, occult bleeding from an additional source is a possible cause of persistent anemia in this patient. This could be due to a second gynecological disorder (e.g. STD, malignancy, endometritis, or endometrial polyp) or a GI disorder (e.g. hemorrhoids, diverticulosis, inflammatory bowel disease, or malignancy). Conditions that could result in poor absorption of oral iron include celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and helicobacter pylori gastritis. @Neet_pg_bot

You are waiting on authorization for hemoglobin electropheresis. Which of the following features on a complete blood count can help distinguish sickle cell anemia from sickle beta thalassemia?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - MCV (Mean Corpuscular Volume): Sickle cell anemia and sickle beta thalassemia are both hemoglobinopathies caused by mutations in the beta-globin gene. However, they have different underlying genetic abnormalities, resulting in distinct red blood cell characteristics that can be detected on a complete blood count (CBC). The mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is a measure of the average volume of red blood cells. In sickle cell anemia, the MCV is typically within the normal range or slightly decreased because the disease primarily affects the structure and function of hemoglobin molecules within the red blood cells. The red blood cells in sickle cell anemia are usually normocytic (normal-sized) or mildly microcytic (smaller than normal). On the other hand, sickle beta thalassemia is a combination of sickle cell trait and beta thalassemia, a disorder characterized by reduced synthesis of beta-globin chains. In sickle beta thalassemia, the MCV is usually more significantly decreased because beta thalassemia leads to smaller red blood cells (microcytosis) due to reduced hemoglobin production. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hemoglobin: Hemoglobin levels may be decreased in both sickle cell anemia and sickle beta thalassemia due to chronic hemolysis and anemia, but this parameter alone cannot distinguish between the two conditions. Option B - MCHC (Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration): MCHC is a measure of the concentration of hemoglobin in a given volume of red blood cells. It is not a distinguishing feature between sickle cell anemia and sickle beta thalassemia, as both conditions can have similar MCHC values. Option D - MCH (Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin): MCH is a measure of the average amount of hemoglobin per red blood cell. Like MCHC, it is not a distinguishing feature between sickle cell anemia and sickle beta thalassemia, as both conditions can have similar MCH values. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D: Irradiation of all RBC products given to the patient Transfusion-associated graft versus host disease (TA-GVHD), which is described in the patient above, is a fatal condition that typically occurs 4-30 days after receipt of a blood transfusion (cellular products and fresh, non-frozen plasma are implicated). In most clinical scenarios, the recipient’s immune system destroys donor lymphocytes following a blood transfusion, preventing the onset of TA-GVHD.
